title: Reflecting on Disaster Relief 2.0 a decade later
html:
Has Humanitarian Information Management improved in the past decade? Has the community found constructive ways to work with, or adopt techniques from, the digital humanitarians? These were the kind of questions I found myself pondering on the 10-year anniversary of the 2011 Disaster Relief 2.0 report (DR2). Had technology really changed humanitarian information sharing in emergencies?

To get an understanding, I collaborated with Kristen Pearn and Sarah A Jabbar to undertake a 10-year review of the report. To keep the scope manageable and a bit novel, we decided to interview the same interviewees*, ask them for their reflections on the report, and determine why each recommendation was or was not implemented. Our report is now available: A Decade Later - Reflecting on Disaster Relief 2.0 - June 2022.

[PDF]

Unfortunately, many of the information management (IM) challenges facing the humanitarian sector a decade ago persist today. They include aggregating and analyzing data inflows from digital humanitarians and affected populations as well as translating the data into actionable insights amid humanitarian crises.

Within ten years, the humanitarian landscape has changed considerably, presenting new and exciting opportunities as well as new risks. We found the interviewees keen to engage in other topics, from localization to burnout; to cyber risks and threats; to the traditional sector’s preparedness efforts; and to its lack of adaptability. The discussions showed that there are multiple underlying issues tethered to the topics discussed in the original report.

Reflecting on the insights shared by the interviewees, one may ask if the humanitarian sectoris at an even bigger precipice. Will the technology that it once got so excited about turn out to be the thing that actually enables more local response and collaboration, and thus truly changes the role of the international humanitarian sector? Only time will tell. Let’s see what the next 10 years bring.

Andrej

* We did the interviewee list slightly to include some more local voices and to ensure the same organizations were represented.
teaser: A review with Kristen Pearn and Sarah A Jabbar finds many information management challenges from Disaster Relief 2.0 still persist ten years later.
seo_description: A decade-later review of the Disaster Relief 2.0 report, interviewing the original participants and others about changes in humanitarian information sharing.
